title: SAKE: Spectral Autodiff Kernel Expansion for Geometric Liouvillian Transport. A Differential-Geometric Framework for Response Transport in Quantum Dynamical Systems
authors: Eric R. Bittner, Carlos Silva-Acuna, Hao Li, Simon Paiva-Ortega
abstract: We introduce the Spectral Autodiff Kernel Expansion (SAKE), a differentiable computational framework for transporting nonlinear spectroscopic response between neighboring quantum dynamical models. Rather than recomputing multidimensional spectra independently for each Hamiltonian or Liouvillian, SAKE constructs local transport expansions about a reference model by combining forward-mode automatic differentiation with Duhamel transport theory. Automatic differentiation generates first-, second-, and third-order derivatives of the parameter-dependent Liouvillian, which are assembled into a pathway transport operator that maps the nonlinear response of a reference model onto neighboring systems. The framework is validated for a four-level excitonic dimer possessing an $su(2)\times su(2)$ symmetry by comparing second- and third-order transported pathway operators with exact projected transport matrices obtained from direct calculations. The third-order expansion accurately reproduces the projected transport operator and its associated pathway mixing. Beyond providing an efficient computational strategy, the transport operator reveals how coherent and dissipative perturbations redistribute amplitude among double-sided Feynman pathways, exposing mechanistic information that is not directly apparent from the nonlinear spectrum. SAKE thereby establishes a differentiable computational framework for nonlinear spectroscopy that supports efficient local parameter exploration, sensitivity analysis, and future inverse-design applications.
summary: This paper introduces SAKE, a novel, differentiable computational framework that uses automatic differentiation and Duhamel theory to efficiently calculate how nonlinear spectroscopic responses change across neighboring quantum models. By constructing a pathway transport operator, the method reveals underlying mechanistic information about amplitude redistribution in quantum dynamics. This greatly enhances the feasibility of local parameter exploration and inverse design in quantum optics.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for an efficient, differentiable method to calculate and transport nonlinear spectroscopic response between neighboring quantum dynamical models.
main_result: The Spectral Autodiff Kernel Expansion (SAKE) framework successfully constructs a pathway transport operator that accurately maps nonlinear response from a reference model to neighboring systems, revealing mechanistic details hidden in the spectrum.
method: It combines forward-mode automatic differentiation with Duhamel transport theory to generate and assemble high-order derivatives of the Liouvillian superoperator, avoiding independent recomputation for each parameter point.
model_or_system: The framework is applied to quantum dynamical systems, specifically validated using a four-level excitonic dimer exhibiting su(2) x su(2) symmetry, governed by a Liouvillian superoperator.
key_observables: Nonlinear spectroscopic response (rephasing spectrum) and the pathway transport operator, which quantifies amplitude redistribution among Feynman pathways.
important_parameters: The order of the Taylor expansion (up to third order) and the control coordinates defining the path in parameter space.
main_assumptions: The model parameters map smoothly to the Liouvillian, and the entire process can be represented as a differentiable computational graph.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the SAKE-DT workflow, showing the sequence from Liouvillian construction to the final observable response via AD and Duhamel assembly, and show reconstructed spectra and transport blocks.
paper_structure: The paper introduces SAKE, details the combination of AD and Duhamel theory to build the transport operator, validates the method on an excitonic dimer, and discusses the physical interpretation of the resulting transport coefficients.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, automated tool for analyzing open quantum systems dynamics, allowing researchers to perform local parameter exploration and sensitivity analysis on complex spectroscopic measurements without prohibitive computational costs.

Stars mark the synthetic targets and the dotted line denotes the imposed dissipative-coupling bound. (b) Relative pathway-state residual versus accepted iteration. FIG. 4. Evolution of the rephasing spectrum during iterative recovery. Direct rephasing spectra on a 64 × 64 frequency grid at four accepted chart centers along the positive-J (orange, upper row) and mixed (green, lower row) trajectories. Coordinates above each panel are (J/ω0, κ/ω0); A/A0 gives the maximum absolute real amplitude relative to the uncoupled spectrum. The plotted signal in each panel is divided by its own maximum to expose changes in line shape.
